Use only if clearly needed; bleeding risk to mother and fetus

summary: Urokinase is a fibrinolytic enzyme that directly converts plasminogen to plasmin to dissolve thrombi. It has been used for acute massive pulmonary embolism, coronary artery thrombosis, and clearance of occluded intravenous catheters. Its principal hazard is bleeding. The original systemic product (Kinlytic) is no longer routinely marketed in the United States; a catheter-clearance form has also been used. Data here are drawn from historical FDA labeling and reference sources rather than a current openFDA label.
indications: Lysis of acute massive pulmonary embolism and PE with unstable hemodynamics
Lysis of coronary artery thrombi associated with acute myocardial infarction (historical)
Restoration of patency to occluded intravenous catheters (low-dose, local instillation)

dosage.d: Loading 4400 IU/kg IV over 10 minutes, then continuous 4400 IU/kg/hour for 12 hours
dosage.n: Historical Kinlytic regimen; followed by heparin once safe

dosage.d: Per catheterization protocol (e.g., bolus then infusion intracoronary)
Instill a volume equal to the catheter lumen of dilute urokinase solution; dwell and aspirate
dosage.n: Low-dose local use; do not force

admin: Reconstitute and administer per protocol; for systemic use give via infusion pump with continuous monitoring
Avoid intramuscular injections and non-essential handling/invasive procedures during therapy
Apply pressure and monitor all puncture/access sites for bleeding
Have means to manage hemorrhage available (e.g., fresh frozen plasma, aminocaproic acid, blood products)
moa: Urokinase is a serine protease that directly activates the endogenous fibrinolytic system by cleaving plasminogen to form plasmin. Plasmin degrades fibrin clots as well as circulating fibrinogen and clotting factors V and VIII, producing thrombolysis and a systemic lytic state. Unlike fibrin-specific agents, it acts on both clot-bound and circulating plasminogen.

absolute: Recent (within ~2-3 months) cerebrovascular accident, intracranial/intraspinal surgery or trauma
Intracranial neoplasm, arteriovenous malformation, or aneurysm
relative: Recent major surgery, organ biopsy, or trauma (within ~10 days)
monitor: Signs of internal or surface bleeding
Vital signs and neurologic status (intracranial bleed)

preg: There are no adequate human data; thrombolytics carry a substantial maternal and fetal bleeding risk, particularly around delivery. Use only if the potential benefit clearly outweighs the risk.
lact: It is not known whether urokinase is excreted in human milk; given its parenteral use in acute settings, the maternal benefit should be weighed against theoretical infant risk.
renal: No specific dosage adjustment is established; evaluate overall bleeding risk.
hepatic: Use with caution; hepatic dysfunction (with reduced clotting factor synthesis) increases the risk of bleeding.

major: Anticoagulants (heparin, warfarin) - markedly increased bleeding risk
Antiplatelet agents (aspirin, clopidogrel, NSAIDs, GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors) - increased bleeding
moderate: Drugs affecting platelet function or coagulation (dextran, dipyridamole)
minor: Aminocaproic/tranexamic acid (antifibrinolytics) - antagonize the therapeutic effect (used to treat overdose bleeding)
interactions.alcohol: Not applicable in the acute setting.
interactions.diagnostics: Induces a systemic lytic state; markedly alters fibrinogen, plasminogen, and fibrin-degradation-product assays.

common: Bleeding (surface oozing, ecchymosis, hematoma at access sites)

monitoring: Continuous observation for bleeding (overt and occult)
Access/puncture sites and any invasive lines
counsel: This is a powerful clot-dissolving medicine given in hospital under close monitoring
Bleeding is the main risk - the team will watch for it and limit needle sticks
Report any bleeding, severe headache, weakness, or vision change immediately
Avoid unnecessary movement and invasive procedures during treatment
pk: Thrombolytic effect begins within minutes of infusion
Lytic effect during infusion; clot lysis over hours
Short, approximately 10-20 minutes (cleared by the liver)
Systemic lytic state may persist several hours after the infusion ends
Refrigerate lyophilized product per labeling; reconstitute immediately before use and do not shake
pearls: NOTE: The systemic urokinase product (Kinlytic) is not currently routinely marketed in the US and returns no current openFDA label; this record is based on historical FDA labeling and reference sources
Directly activates plasminogen (no antigenicity issues of streptokinase) - dissolves both clot-bound and circulating plasminogen, producing a systemic lytic state
Bleeding is the dominant hazard - avoid IM injections and non-essential punctures, and screen carefully for contraindications
Antifibrinolytics (aminocaproic or tranexamic acid) plus blood products are used to treat serious bleeding
Low-dose local instillation is used to clear occluded IV catheters with minimal systemic effect
missed: Not applicable - administered as a clinician-controlled infusion or single catheter instillation, not on a fixed dosing schedule.
overdose: Overdose or excessive fibrinolysis manifests as serious bleeding. Management is to stop the infusion, apply local pressure, and provide volume/blood-product resuscitation; fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate, and an antifibrinolytic agent (aminocaproic or tranexamic acid) are used to reverse the lytic state and control hemorrhage.
